at.step: Reveal: choosing a partition key means choosing what retention can drop
Reveal: two different signals for two different moments
Reveal: overhead of too many partitions

items.item: With partition pruning enabled, the planner proves a partition can't match the WHERE clause and excludes it from the plan
Partition pruning can also be performed during execution, visible via Subplans Removed in EXPLAIN
Too many partitions can mean longer query planning times and higher memory consumption

at.step: Reveal: overhead of too many partitions

items.item: Dropping an individual partition is far faster than a bulk operation and avoids the VACUUM overhead a bulk DELETE causes

at.step: Reveal: DROP vs. DELETE for retention

items.item: Clustered tables sort data in storage blocks by clustered columns instead of splitting the table into separate physical objects

items.item: The plan-time pruning measurement uses a 60-partition table, large enough to make the contrast dramatic and realistic rather than a toy 2-3-partition example

The run-time pruning measurement genuinely forces a generic plan via plan_cache_mode, reproducing a precondition from topic 27's own PostgreSQL execution-time pruning work rather than accidentally measuring plan-time pruning of a literal-substituted plan

The overhead-of-many-partitions measurement isolates partition count as the only variable by loading identical data into a partitioned and an unpartitioned table and comparing planning time specifically, not execution time

at.step: Reveal: overhead of too many partitions

items.item: The retention measurement uses a realistic row count (1,000,000 per partition) and explicitly notes the additional VACUUM overhead DELETE would still need beyond the measured DELETE time itself, rather than understating DELETE's real total cost

at.step: Reveal: DROP vs. DELETE for retention

items.item: The warehouse-clustering contrast is sourced and explicitly disclosed as not independently measured, consistent with this chapter's honest-gap pattern for claims about systems not installed on this sandbox

The distinction between constraint exclusion (legacy inheritance, plan-time only) and partition pruning (declarative partitioning, plan-time and run-time) drawn out as a related but separate mechanism, not conflated with pruning itself
A closing check that requires reasoning about partition count directly (24 total, 23 pruned) rather than re-testing the exact measured numbers from the reveals

Four distinct mechanisms (plan-time pruning, run-time pruning, partition-count overhead, retention via DROP) kept separate in the recap rather than blended into one vague 'partitioning is good' takeaway

The choice between range, list and hash partitioning tied explicitly to the predicates queries actually use and to retention policy, rather than presented as three equally-likely options with no selection criterion

Every locally-measured claim in this topic reuses the existing PostgreSQL 16.15 sandbox instance rather than requiring new infrastructure, consistent with the chapter's established measurement environment
